# Consent and ethics of experiments on people (`informed_consent_research_ethics`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: helped by controlled_trial
- Core idea: Before trying an unproven treatment on a person, tell them what is known and what is risked and get their free agreement; do not experiment on those who cannot refuse (prisoners, slaves, orphans, the poor of a hospital) merely because they are available. Require prior evidence to justify the risks, independent review, a plan for monitoring harm and clear stopping rules. Respect withdrawal and record outcomes including deaths. Besides being right, this is what keeps a trial from ending in a riot or a murder charge and makes its results believed. The Hippocratic rule 'help, or at least do no harm' gives the argument a respected ancient footing.
- Pitfalls:
  - Treating the consent of a master, parent, abbot or prince as the consent of the subject
  - Quoting 'first, do no harm' as part of the Hippocratic Oath; the wording comes from Epidemics I and the Latin tag is modern
  - Citing Jenner as a model: he inoculated an eight-year-old servant's son and then deliberately exposed him to smallpox
  - Heroic self-experiment as proof: one person is no trial, and a dead player teaches nobody
- History: greece: c. 400 BC – Hippocratic Oath and Epidemics I: act for the benefit of the sick, do no harm; india: c. 1st–2nd c. AD – oath of the medical student in the Charaka Samhita; china: c. 652 – Sun Simiao, 'On the Absolute Sincerity of Great Physicians': treat all patients alike, without regard to rank or reward; islamic: 9th c. – al-Ruhawi, Ethics of the Physician; europe: 1721 – smallpox inoculation tried on condemned Newgate prisoners in return for pardon; 1803 Percival, Medical Ethics; 1900 Prussian directive requiring consent; 1947 Nuremberg Code after the Doctors' Trial; americas: 1900 – Walter Reed's yellow fever volunteers sign written consent in Cuba; 1932–1972 Tuskegee syphilis study, the standard example of abuse; global: 1964 – Declaration of Helsinki
- Read:
  - Nuremberg Military Tribunals, The Nuremberg Code (1947)
  - Albert R. Jonsen, A Short History of Medical Ethics (2000)
  - Susan E. Lederer, Subjected to Science: Human Experimentation in America before the Second World War (1995)
